entities.summary:
Gjirokastër, often hailed as the 'City of Stone,' is an exceptionally preserved Ottoman-era city in southern Albania, strategically situated on the slopes of the Drino Valley overlooking the Drina River. Its historical importance is profound, primarily stemming from its unique architectural heritage, which exemplifies a rare type of Ottoman town planning and building style, featuring distinctive tower-houses (kulla) and cobbled streets. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2005, Gjirokastër offers a tangible connection to centuries of Balkan history, serving as a living museum of Ottoman urban and social structures that flourished from the 17th to the 19th centuries.

The city's origins trace back to antiquity, with evidence of Illyrian settlements, but its distinct character solidified under Ottoman rule, beginning in 1417. By the 17th century, Gjirokastër had developed into a thriving administrative and trading center, its prosperity reflected in the construction of its monumental castle, which dominates the city skyline, and the proliferation of its characteristic two- and three-story stone houses. These kulla, fortified dwellings built for prominent families, are distinguished by their defensive features, elaborate interior decorations, and functional design, including separate living quarters for extended families. The city also played a role in the Albanian National Awakening, and notably, it is the birthplace of Albania's long-time communist dictator, Enver Hoxha, adding another layer to its complex modern history.
